I didn't find a direct answer. No result gives PVWatts output for Santa Fe's December tilted-array irradiance in kWh/m²/day.

- **Santa Fe, third-party estimate:** Profilesolar reports winter output of about 3.85 kWh per kW of installed PV per day, using NASA POWER hourly data. It's an energy-per-kW figure, not irradiance, and it isn't from PVWatts. It also recommends a south tilt of about 32 degrees. (During autumn, the production drops a bit to around 5.39 kilowatt-hours per day and in winter it falls further to about 3.85 kilowatt-hours per day.; tilt them towards south at an angle of 32 degrees from horizontal level.)
- **New Mexico statewide, PVWatts v8:** TheGreenWatt cites a December low of about 4.4 peak sun hours per day for the state. That is a state average, not Santa Fe, and it isn't clear whether it is tilted or horizontal. (New Mexico's solar resource peaks in June at 8.07 peak sun hours per day and bottoms out in December at 4.4.)
- **Other PVWatts reports:** The results include PVWatts printouts for other sites, such as Kirksville, Missouri, and Mercer Island, Washington. Their December rows show the format PVWatts uses, but they don't cover Santa Fe.

To get the exact figure, run PVWatts at the Santa Fe coordinates (about 35.69° N, 105.94° W) with your intended tilt and azimuth. Its monthly table reports the plane-of-array irradiance in kWh/m²/day.

Web search results for query: "off-grid solar design worst month peak sun hours New Mexico winter tilt latitude+15"

Links: [{"title":"Solar Lighting: Making Steps Off-Grid towards a Sustainable Future","url":"https://continuingeducation.bnpmedia.com/courses/selux/solar-lighting-making-steps-offgrid-towards-a-sustainable-future/9"},{"title":"Optimising array angle","url":"https://forum.solar-electric.com/discussion/comment/85080"},{"title":"Optimising array angle","url":"https://forum.solar-electric.com/discussion/comment/85070"},{"title":"STTC%20062326%20Item%205%20Driven%20Design%20of%20a%20Stand Alone%20PV%20System%20to%20Support%20Residential%20Loads%20on%20the%20Navajo%20Nation","url":"https://www.nmlegis.gov/(X(1)S(0d3dh1cyocbnztybqvja2dch))/handouts/STTC%20062326%20Item%205%20Driven%20Design%20of%20a%20Stand-Alone%20PV%20System%20to%20Support%20Residential%20Loads%20on%20the%20Navajo%20Nation.pdf"},{"title":"irradiance estimator","url":"https://www.surgepv.com/tools/irradiance-estimator"},{"title":"Results 1 to 15 of 15","url":"https://www.4x4community.co.za/forum/showthread.php/221910-Perfect-tilt-for-solar-panels"},{"title":"Back to Blog","url":"https://www.surgepv.com/blog/off-grid-solar-system-sizing-calculator"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/works/9741926"},{"title":"samplecontents.library.ph","url":"https://samplecontents.library.ph/en-practical_action/Energy/Solar%20energy/off-grid-solar-install-manual/page29.html"}]

The search turned up the design logic but no New Mexico-specific monthly sun-hour table, so you'll need NREL PVWatts or NSRDB data for an exact figure.

- **Critical month:** One source says off-grid systems are sized for the month with the lowest irradiation, which is also the month with the longest nights. It names December as the critical month for a northern site near 45° latitude. Off grid systems are most concerned with optimizing tilt angle to achieve the highest minimum irradiation value during the critical design month. A New Mexico site would likely follow the same logic, but no result confirmed that for New Mexico.
- **Winter tilt for New Mexico latitudes:** A New Mexico Legislature handout on a Navajo Nation off-grid design uses a Navajo Nation latitude of 36° to 38°. It recommends a fixed tilt of about 37°. For adjustable mounts, it suggests a winter tilt of latitude + 15°, which works out to roughly 47° to 52°. Winter: 𝜃𝜃 = 𝜙𝜙 + 15°, with the document's note that this improves winter performance for off-grid systems.
- **Why steeper helps in winter:** A Practical Action installation manual says a steeper panel catches more winter sunlight when the sun sits lower, and that off-grid systems should aim for maximum winter capture because that is when batteries are hardest to keep charged. For year round electrical load, an offgrid solar system should be installed in a way that captures maximum solar irradiation during winter.
- **Magnitude of the gain:** A forum user's PVWatts comparison for a different site showed about a 10% December gain from a +15° winter tilt. That is an anecdote, not a New Mexico benchmark.
- **Sizing caution:** A sizing guide warns that arrays sized for summer output are a common cause of off-grid failures, and it treats winter peak sun hours as the key input. It does not give a New Mexico value. The cause is almost always the same: the array was sized for summer production, not December.
- **Data source:** The SurgePV calculator reports state averages from NREL's NSRDB, but its displayed values are for California, so I would not use them for New Mexico. The same page recommends NREL PVWatts for site-specific data.

content.text:
## First-principles approach

Two independent numbers are needed: **battery kWh** (how much stored energy covers you through dark/cloudy stretches) and **panel W** (how fast you can refill that battery during the worst month of the year). They're sized against different constraints — autonomy for the battery, worst-month insolation for the array — so treat them separately.

### 1. What the battery actually has to deliver

1.5 kWh/day is presumably measured at the loads (lights, fridge, laptop charging, etc.), which run through an inverter if any are AC. Inverter + wiring losses are typically ~10%, so the battery itself must supply:

**1.5 kWh / 0.90 ≈ 1.67 kWh/day**

### 2. Battery bank sizing (autonomy × DoD)

```
Battery (nameplate) = (daily energy × autonomy days) / depth of discharge
```

LiFePO4 can cycle to ~100% DoD, but designing to ~80% DoD meaningfully extends cycle life and leaves voltage headroom — worth it for a bank you can't easily swap in the backcountry.

```
= (1.67 kWh × 3 days) / 0.80
≈ 6.3 kWh nameplate (~5 kWh usable)
```

**→ Target a 6–7 kWh LiFePO4 bank** (e.g., 48V ×130–150 Ah, or four 12V/100 Ah units reconfigured to 48V with a bit of extra Ah). This gives ~5–6 kWh usable at a conservative DoD.

### 3. Panel array sizing (worst-month insolation, not annual average)

This is the step people get wrong — sizing off an annual-average sun-hour number means the system fails exactly when you need it most, in December. New Mexico's high desert has an outstanding solar resource, but the sun angle is still low and days are short in winter, so December is the governing month.

Rough NREL-based figures for north-central NM (~35–36°N) put December production around **3.85–4.3 kWh delivered per kW of installed panel per day** for a south-facing array near latitude-tilt-to-winter-tilt (32°–50°) — this figure already bakes in typical system losses (wiring, charge-controller/inverter efficiency, soiling, temperature derate), so it maps fairly directly to battery-delivered energy per installed DC watt.

```
Minimum array (kW) = daily energy needed / worst-month production factor
= 1.67 kWh / ~4.0 kWh/kW/day
≈ 0.42 kW = ~420 W
```

That's the bare-minimum array that breaks even on an average December day — it has zero margin for a multi-day winter storm, panel aging (~0.5%/yr), or the charge taper that happens as a LiFePO4 bank approaches full SoC. Off-grid design convention applies a 1.4–1.6× margin on top of the worst-month minimum for exactly this reason (this is also the single most common cause of off-grid system failure — sizing to summer or annual-average output instead of the winter design month).

```
420 W × ~1.5 ≈ 600–650 W, round up for practical module sizes
```

**→ Target a 600–800 W array** (e.g., two 350–400 W modules), south-facing, tilted steep (~45–50°, i.e., latitude + 10–15°) to favor winter harvest over summer surplus — summer will be massively oversupplied either way given NM's resource, which is fine; winter is the constraint that matters.

### Bottom line

| Component | Spec |
|---|---|
| Panel array | **600–800 W** (south-facing, ~45–50° tilt) |
| Battery bank | **6–7 kWh nameplate LiFePO4** (~5–6 kWh usable @ 80% DoD) |

This covers 3 days of autonomy at 1.5 kWh/day with a realistic margin for December's short days and the occasional multi-day overcast spell, without being wildly oversized for a 2-person cabin load. One caveat: these insolation numbers are regional estimates, not your exact coordinates — before buying hardware, run your actual lat/long through NREL's PVWatts (free, no coding needed) at your intended tilt to confirm the December daily output number and adjust the array size proportionally if it comes in notably lower than ~4 kWh/kW/day.

Sources:
- [Profilesolar — Santa Fe solar production estimates](https://profilesolar.com/locations/United-States/Santa-Fe/)
- [TheGreenWatt — New Mexico peak sun hours](https://www.thegreenwatt.com/new-mexico-peak-sun-hours/)
- [NM Legislature handout — Stand-alone PV system design, Navajo Nation](https://www.nmlegis.gov/handouts/STTC%20062326%20Item%205%20Driven%20Design%20of%20a%20Stand-Alone%20PV%20System%20to%20Support%20Residential%20Loads%20on%20the%20Navajo%20Nation.pdf)
- [SurgePV — Off-grid solar system sizing calculator](https://www.surgepv.com/blog/off-grid-solar-system-sizing-calculator)
